DeepWalk can use Asynchronous Stochastic Gradient Descent (ASGD) across multiple worker threads without parameter locks because its optimization problem is unusually tolerant to stale, conflicting updates. DeepWalk learns node embeddings from many short random-walk-generated Skip-gram training pairs, and each update touches only a small subset of the embedding parameters. As a result, concurrent workers usually update different rows of the embedding matrices, so write conflicts are relatively sparse. Even when conflicts occur, the updates are noisy but still approximately unbiased stochastic gradient steps, and the objective is nonconvex and highly redundant, so small amounts of asynchrony do not materially degrade the learned representation.

More specifically, DeepWalk’s training signal comes from local co-occurrence statistics in random walks rather than from a tightly coupled global constraint. That means the model does not require exact serial consistency to preserve the geometry of the embedding space. In practice, the asynchronous updates mainly improve throughput by reducing synchronization overhead, while the learned embeddings remain good enough for downstream tasks such as Node Classification and Link Prediction. This is why the original DeepWalk implementation reported that lock-free parallel training scaled well and did not noticeably hurt predictive performance.

In short: DeepWalk works well with lock-free ASGD because its sparse, local, stochastic Skip-gram updates are robust to occasional parameter staleness and collisions, so parallelism increases speed more than it harms embedding quality.
